My leading suspicion would be that this is related to outliers . Have you run your data through outlie() to see what comes out. If its outliers, with this much data, you might consider automating (in a loop over individuals) some kind of outlier rejection threshold, kind of like in vignette('error') but with plot=FALSE for speed.

Let me know if this doesn't address the issue.

Best,
Chris

On the other hand, there are no obvious outliers of straight line distances in the months with the extreme ctmm daily speed estimates (346-622 km/ day). The maximum SLD speeds in these months are nearly always lower than 0.09 m/s and only reached 1.3 m/s in one of these months.
Filtering by DOF also does not help, since the point estimate is very large along with the confidence interval.
What else can I check?

Thanks again!

Best,
Maik

messages.subject_clean: Question regarding ctmm model fitting on CPF tracks
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a question regarding the ctmm model fitting for a central-place foraging species (in R). I have a dataset of a few thousand tracks so I am looking for ways for dealing with a list of telemetry objects.

As other central-place foragers in their reproductive period, individuals are going back and forth to their nesting site. Due to behavioral heterogeneity, individuals differ greatly in terms of trips' length and duration.

So far I explored the ctmm() function and tried to fit a periodic-mean process, using the *omega* and *circle* parameters (see below). However, the autocorrelation structure is very variable inter-individually.

All tracks have been delineated, meaning that each trip represents a single departure and arrival to the nesting site.

ctmm(mean = "periodic", sigma=30 %#% "km^2",tau=c(5 %#% "hours",1 %#% "days"), CPF = TRUE,
          omega = 0.000001, isotropic = T, range = F, circle = 0.0005)

The model fits well for short trips;

However, the function doesn't fit well longer tracks;

I know that the standard OUF model has been applied to other central-place foragers, despite the intrinsic circular pattern (e.g. Mitchell et al. 2019; https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0219357). I am then wondering if using a stationary variance model would be preferable in my case since the heterogeneity in my dataset is so important?

However, is the use of the OUF model, or other "asymptotic" assumed variance model, would "overcorrect" the end of each trip (i.e. location being closer to the colony)? This would be seen as a "conservative" approach since indeed space use around the colony is most likely very variable (at least according to my tracks i.e. no specific angle to departure).

I am using R 4.0.0, ctmm 0.5.10.

Thanks in advance,

/Phil

messages.subject_clean: Question regarding ctmm model fitting on CPF tracks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

The longer variograms look very much like an initial diffusion/dispersal behavior, followed by a more directed return behavior. This is non-stationary (behavioral switching) and for the moment the models in ctmm are all stationary. Non-stationary modeling is planned, but right now I am focused on hierarchical models and meta-analysis.

What kind of results are you hoping to get? My recommendations would depend on the scale of inference.

Notes:
The ctmm() argument CPF=TRUE no longer does anything, as I no longer refer to those models as CPF, because they only mimic CPF behavior for short tracks of data as you have carefully noticed (is CPF still in some help files?). I replaced that argument with the omega argument, but the way to do that manually would look more like

ctmm(tau=c(5%#%"hours",5%#%"hours"),omega=2*pi/(1%#%"days"),...)

with repeated tau values when omega!=0. Hopefully, its just ignoring the difference when you provide two different tau and an omega. In current versions of the package model selection should be able to find the oscillatory model if it fits better, even if you don't specify it initially.
Also, I don't think circle!=0 and range=FALSE are compatible options (there should be a warning from that somewhere?). From your plot, it looks like range=FALSE is being ignored in favor of circle.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thank you for your quick reply.

Our objective is to quantify the home range size (HR) of different seabird colonies, which are separated from each other by less than 20km. The temporal scale of the study is ca. 1 month.

We are also predicting that segregation occurs among the colony's HR, due to seascape structure. Processes are expected to occur in a range of ca. 30km. Interestingly, the variograms' asymptote is often located around that 30km threshold.

I have adapted the model based on your recommendations;

ctmm(sigma=30 %#% "km^2",tau=c(5%#%"hours",5%#%"hours"),omega=2*pi/(1%#%"days"), isotropic = T, circle = T)

The fit improved on some trips but underestimated the semi-variance in others. Likely due to the high heterogeneity, many models didn't converge or give odd confidence intervals for parameters like speed and T[period](hours).

On the other hand, fits from the OUf models gave sensible results, and the confidence interval overlap often the majority of the lags (see below for an example of short/long trips);

Based on these patterns, I am then tempted to prefer the non-circular model. In the case where the model is assumed to be asymptotic, I am however wondering about the bandwidth effect at greater lags (e.g. >3.5 hrs for the two first figures and at > 20 hrs in the 3rd one above) and on the resulting HR estimates?

Thanks in advance, best, /Phil

NB. You are totally right, the CPF argument is not in the current help file. Also, I don't have noticed any warnings regarding the simultaneous use of the circle!=0 and range=FALSE arguments while implemented in the ctmm(), ctmm.guess() and ctmm.fit() functions.

Hi Phil,

Those plots look pretty good, all considering.
Since the tracks are so short, you might consider CI="Gauss" in variogram(), which provides more exact empirical variogram CIs.
For home-range estimation you want a lot of range crossings to get a good effective sample size (the two quantities are similar in size). I'd be concerned with statistical efficiency on short tracks. The default method in ctmm.fit/ctmm.select ("pHREML") is pretty good down to around DOF[area] of ~5, while ctmm.boot can push that down to ~3, but ctmm.boot is very slow. Do you need per-track estimates, or can you do per-bird estimates?
Normally, I let ctmm.select decide whether or not isotropic=TRUE and circle!=0, but I have found issues with AIC/BIC in short tracks. AIC/BIC are only assured to work well asymptotically. I have implemented some alternative ICs that don't make asymptotic assumptions/approximations ("HSCV" for coarse-scale performance selection and "LOOCV" for fine-scale performance selection), but I haven't found that "HSCV" works that much better than AIC/BIC.
What was odd about the speed and period CIs on selected models?
I'm not sure what you mean by "bandwidth effect at greater lags".
Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

In non-independent data, the effective sample sizes (DOFs) for different statistics can be fairly different. DOF[H] is for the bandwidth 'H' and DOF[area] is for the area estimates. For DOFs, what ctmm reports are the equivalent number of IID locations to obtain an estimate of that precision in its sampling distribution. E.g., you might have 30 sampled locations, but as far as uncertainty in the area estimate, it is as if you only had 4 locations sampled, because those 30 locations are very similar, as they were sampled closely in time.
An average DOF of 4.3 per trip x 4.0 trips per bird should hopefully work out to ~17 per individual, which isn't terrible for the default estimator.
I'm not sure what you mean about using DOF[area] in the AKDE calculation, but it is used for the AKDE CIs. Population AKDEs are in the pipeline and will be informed by that information too.
I'm a little unclear on the bad CIs. Are these bad CIs occurring in the top model selected via ctmm.select? If so, I could take a closer look that those examples. If they are not in the selected model, then I wouldn't worry about it. Parameter estimates aren't expected to have good CIs if those parameters can't be supported by the data in model selection.
I'm still not sure I quite follow you on the "bandwidth effect at a greater lag", but I do agree that the autocorrelation model is not perfect at capturing the return behavior. However, it does appear to have the asymptote and decay to asymptote well captured, which are the more important features to model for home-range estimation.
Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am working on a central-place foraging species and have a dataset of a few thousand tracks.

I am investigating the presence of segregation among the colony's home range. I am then modelling the spatial distribution at the individual-level, for thereafter testing segregation by randomization procedure using the overlap() function (i.e. over colony affiliation of the individuals).

Individual tracking was first segmented into foraging trips, in order to reduce the weight of the numerous localization at the colony between the foraging trips. Since the overlap() function doesn't appear to be reliable when implemented with the average distributions (e.g. from mean.UD), I am searching for the most optimal way of aggregating data within the individual stratum. So far, I am considering continuous time between each individual's trip, and by removing the "extra" localisation at the colony (i.e. except the departure and arrival points to the colony). In other words, we have a regular interval of 10 min between every two locations within individuals, having thus a maximum of 10 min at the colony before the next trip.

By doing so, and since periodicity is low in the data, the ctmm.fit() give sensible results. However, I am curious to know if another (proper?) way is existing for dealing with such data?

Furthermore, I have noticed that sometimes the variograms doesn't show all the lags, although numbers occur in the input data frame. I suspect a DOF effect since that one is < 1 (according to https://rdrr.io/cran/ctmm/src/R/variogram.R). However, would the estimates from such structure be reliable?

Many thanks again, best /Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

Proper CIs on mean UDs are in the short-term pipeline, but I don't know what time constraints you have, so don't wait for me.
ctmm is currently limited to stationary processes (with the simple exception of non-stationary mean functions), and that will be a longer-term upgrade. So it is a good idea to segment the data into individual behaviors before fitting a stationary model. If I understand what you are doing correctly, there does not need to be a maximum threshold of time between trips. You just want to have the nesting behavior removed.
If you change the fraction argument of plot.variogram, it can show all of the lags. Alternatively, you can use the slider in zoom().
Best,
Chris

On Tuesday, June 30, 2020 at 10:18:25 AM UTC-4, PhilB wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I am working on a central-place foraging species and have a dataset of a few thousand tracks.
>
> I am investigating the presence of segregation among the colony's home range. I am then modelling the spatial distribution at the individual-level, for thereafter testing segregation by randomization procedure using the overlap() function (i.e. over colony affiliation of the individuals).
>
> Individual tracking was first segmented into foraging trips, in order to reduce the weight of the numerous localization at the colony between the foraging trips. Since the overlap() function doesn't appear to be reliable when implemented with the average distributions (e.g. from mean.UD), I am searching for the most optimal way of aggregating data within the individual stratum. So far, I am considering continuous time between each individual's trip, and by removing the "extra" localisation at the colony (i.e. except the departure and arrival points to the colony). In other words, we have a regular interval of 10 min between every two locations within individuals, having thus a maximum of 10 min at the colony before the next trip.
>
> By doing so, and since periodicity is low in the data, the ctmm.fit() give sensible results. However, I am curious to know if another (proper?) way is existing for dealing with such data?
>
> Furthermore, I have noticed that sometimes the variograms doesn't show all the lags, although numbers occur in the input data frame. I suspect a DOF effect since that one is < 1 (according to https://rdrr.io/cran/ctmm/src/R/variogram.R). However, would the estimates from such structure be reliable?
>
>
> Many thanks again, best /Phil
